'''Samar Mubarakmand''' ([[Urdu]]: {{URDU|ثمر مبارک مند}}; born 17 September 1942) is a Pakistani [[nuclear physicist]], known for his research in [[gamma spectroscopy]] and the development of the [[Pakistan Research Reactor#Charged Particle Accelerator|Charged Particle Accelerator]] at the [[Pakistan Institute of Nuclear Science & Technology]] (PINSTECH).<ref name="N.M. Butt international Congress on Radiation Education"/>

As of 2026, he is leading the mineral exploration efforts in the [[Chiniot District|Chiniot]] district, serving as the chairman of the Punjab Mineral Company.<ref name="Dawn News, Kiani">{{cite news|last1=Kiani|first1=Khaliq|title=Breakthrough in coal power|url=https://www.dawn.com/news/1077175|access-date=4 June 2015|agency=Dawn News|publisher=Dawn News, Kiani|date=4 June 2015|archive-date=3 March 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160303232051/http://www.dawn.com/news/1077175|url-status=live}}</ref>

== Early life and education ==
Mubarakmand was born on 17 September 1942, in [[Rawalpindi]] in the [[Punjab Province (British India)|Punjab Province]] of [[British India]] into a [[Muslims|Muslim]] family that originally hailed from the [[Hoshiarpur District]].<ref name="Pakistan Academy of Sciences"/> He was educated in [[Lahore]] and graduated from [[St. Anthony's High School (Lahore)|St. Anthony's High School]] in 1956.<ref name="Pakistan Academy of Sciences">{{Cite web |title=Samar Mubarakmand |website=Pakistan Academy of Sciences |url=http://www.paspk.org/fellow-profile/?fellowID=82 |access-date=7 September 2019 |archive-date=24 September 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200924062410/https://www.paspk.org/fellow-profile/?fellowID=82 |url-status=live }}</ref>

After passing university entrance examinations, he enrolled at [[Government College University, Lahore|Government College University]] (GCU), where he studied physics under [[Tahir Hussain (physicist)|Tahir Hussain]].<ref name="Nazaria-e-Pakistan Trust">{{cite web|last1=Asim|first1=Khalid Mahmood|title=Famous Scientists|url=http://www.nazariapak.info/Famous-Pakistani/Scientists.php|publisher=Nazaria-e-Pakistan Trust|access-date=2 June 2015|archive-date=3 May 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200503133406/http://nazariapak.info/Famous-Pakistani/Scientists.php|url-status=live}}</ref> During university, Mubarakmand was a swimmer and represented GCU at the [[National Games of Pakistan]]. In 1960, he graduated with a [[Bachelor of Science]] (BSc) in [[physics]], concentrating in [[experimental physics]] with a minor in mathematics.<ref name="Nust Science Society">{{Cite web |last=Hasan |first=Osama |date=2010-06-23 |title=An Interview with Dr. Samar Mubarakmand |url=http://irnustian.com/2010/06/an-interview-with-dr-samar-mubarakmand/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100628150605/http://irnustian.com/2010/06/an-interview-with-dr-samar-mubarakmand/ |archive-date=2010-06-28 |access-date=2026-04-08 |website=irnustian.com}}</ref>

He researched experimental physics under Hussain and built an experimental apparatus for his master's thesis. His thesis included work on gamma‑ray spectrometry, and he conducted an experiment witnessed by nuclear physicist [[Denys Wilkinson]] as part of his master's programme. Wilkinson invited Mubarakmand to visit the [[University of Oxford]] to pursue further study in experimental physics.<ref name="Nust Science Society"/>

In 1962, Mubarakmand received an [[Master of Science]] (MSc) in physics after completing his thesis, ''Construction of a Gamma-Ray Spectrometer''.<ref name="N.M. Butt international Congress on Radiation Education">{{cite web|last1=Butt|first1=N.M.|author-link1=N. M. Butt|title=Nuclear Radiation & Nuclear Science & Technology in Pakistan|url=http://pakdef.org/nuclear-radiation-education-and-nuclear-science-and-technology-in-pakistan/|publisher=N.M. Butt international Congress on Radiation Education|access-date=2 June 2015|location=Debrecen, Hungary|date=25 August 2002|archive-date=24 March 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170324165328/http://pakdef.org/nuclear-radiation-education-and-nuclear-science-and-technology-in-pakistan/|url-status=dead}}</ref> The same year, he joined the [[Pakistan Atomic Energy Commission]] (PAEC) and received a scholarship to study at Oxford, where he joined Wilkinson's group. Mubarakmand helped prepare and commission a 22‑million‑volt [[particle accelerator]]. He also studied [[linear accelerator]]s and, after returning to [[Pakistan]], built one.<ref name="Computer Center of Planning Commission of Pakistan">{{cite news|title=Dr. Samar Mubarakmand (N.I, H.I, S.I)|url=http://pc.gov.pk/|access-date=4 June 2015|agency=Planning Commission|publisher=Computer Center of Planning Commission of Pakistan|date=26 December 2008|location=Islamabad Pakistan|pages=1|archive-date=1 December 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201201003113/https://www.pc.gov.pk/|url-status=live}}</ref> Besides his studies, he played cricket as a fast bowler for the [[Oxford University Cricket Club]].<ref name="Nust Science Society" />

During his doctoral studies on nuclear structure at the University of Oxford, Mubarakmand developed and refined a technique for the spectroscopy of fast neutrons released during the nuclear reactions under investigation. This technique has direct applications in conducting cold tests of nuclear devices. In 1966, he completed his [[doctoral thesis]] under Wilkinson and was awarded a [[Doctor of Philosophy]] (DPhil) in experimental [[nuclear physics]].<ref name="Special report, Jang">{{cite web|last1=Shaikh|first1=F.D|title=The galaxy of Pakistani scientists|url=http://jang.com.pk/thenews/jul2009-weekly/us-10-07-2009/p5.htm|publisher=Special report, Jang|access-date=3 June 2015|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304191314/http://jang.com.pk/thenews/jul2009-weekly/us-10-07-2009/p5.htm|archive-date=4 March 2016}}</ref><ref name="Pakistan Herald">{{cite news | url=http://pakistanherald.com/Profile/Dr-Samar-Mubarak-Mand-1283 | work=Pakistan Herald | title=Dr. Samar Mubarakmand | archive-date=19 February 2018 | access-date=8 March 2011 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180219202211/http://www.pakistanherald.com/profile/dr-samar-mubarak-mand-1283 | url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="Nust Science Society, 2012">{{cite web|title=Dr. Samar Mubarakmand|date=29 August 2012|url=https://nustscienceblog.wordpress.com/2012/08/29/dr-samar-mubarakmand-1942-onwards/|publisher=Nust Science Society|access-date=2 June 2015|archive-date=24 December 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161224033252/https://nustscienceblog.wordpress.com/2012/08/29/dr-samar-mubarakmand-1942-onwards/|url-status=live}}</ref>

== Pakistan Atomic Energy Commission (PAEC) ==
{{See also|Project-706}}
Upon completing his doctoral research in [[Fast-neutron reactor|fast neutron spectrometry]], Mubarakmand was appointed to head the Diagnostic Group of the [[Pakistan Atomic Energy Commission]] (PAEC). Drawing on his experience with high‑energy accelerators, he converted a neutron generator available at PAEC to study nuclear structure and fast [[neutron scattering]].

In 1974, he completed research on fast neutron‑induced reactions and developed experimental techniques for neutron spectroscopy. This work resulted in several publications in the journals ''Nuclear Physics'' and ''Nuclear Instruments and Methods'' (North‑Holland).<ref>a) A Fast Neutron Time-of-Flight Spectrometer - S. Mubarakmand, N.A. Khan and P.K. Maher - Nuclear Instruments and Methods 86 (1970) 149-155
b) Neutron Detection Efficiency of an Organic Scintillator - S. Mubarakmand and M. Anwar - Nuclear Instruments and Methods 93 (1971) 515-518
c) Aspects of α-Emission from the Bombardment of 58Ni with 14.7 MeV Neutrons - N.A Khan, S. Mubarakmand and Mahmud Ahmad - Nuclear Physics A202 (1973) 123-126
d) Cross-Section Measurements with a Neutron Generator - S. Mubarakmand, M. Ahmad, M. Anwar and M.S. Chaudhry - Nuclear Instruments and Methods 115 (1974) 345-347</ref>

From 1974 to 1977, he served on temporary attachment as director of the Center for Advanced Studies in Physics (CASP) at [[Government College University, Lahore]]. During this period, he developed an interest in applications of [[solid-state nuclear track detector|solid‑state track detectors]]. In 1976, he presented this work at an international conference at the [[Max Planck Institute]] in Munich.<ref>a) Absolute Determination of Uranium Concentration in Rocks by Gamma-Ray Spectroscopy — S. Mubarakmand, Parvez Chaudhary and F.I. Nagi — Nuclear Instruments and Methods 140 (1977) 133–135
b) Application of Glass Solid State Nuclear Track Detectors in the Measurement of the Charged Particle Fission Cross-Section of Uranium — S. Mubarakmand, Khalid Rashid, Parvez Chaudhary and Hameed A. Khan — Nuclear Instruments and Methods 147 (1977) 279–281
c) Etching of Glass Solid State Nuclear Track Detectors in Aqueous Solutions of (NH4) HF2, NaOH and KOH — Hameed A. Khan, R.A. Akber, A. Waheed, P. Chaudhry and S. Mubarakmand — Int. Journal of Applied Radiation and Isotopes, Vol. 29 (1978) 229–232
d) Some Characteristic Differences Between the Etch Pits due to Radon and Thoron Alpha Particles in CA80-115 and LR-115 Cellulose Nitrate Track Detectors — S. Mubarakmand — Int. Journal of Applied Radiation and Isotopes, 1977, Vol. 28, 727–731</ref><ref>a) New Etchants for Soda Lime Glass Track Detectors — Hameed A. Khan, R.A. Akber, A. Waheed, P. Chaudhry and S. Mubarakmand — Proceedings of the 9th Int. Conf. on SSNTD (Munich, 1976), edited by F. Granzfer, E. Schopper, Pergamon Press (1978)
b) The Use of CA80-15 and LR-115 Cellulose Nitrate Track Detectors for Discrimination Between Radon and Thoron — H.A. Khan, R.A. Akber, A. Waheed, M. Afzal, P. Chaudhry, S. Mubarakmand and F.I. Nagi — Proceedings of the 9th Inter. Conf. on SSNTD (Munich, 1976), edited by F. Granzer, E. Schopper and H.G. Paretzche, Pergamon Press (1978)
c) The Measurement of Helium‑Ion‑Induced Fission Cross‑Section of Uranium by Glass Track Detectors — S. Mubarakmand, P. Chaudhry, K. Rashid, R.A. Akber and H.A. Khan — Proceedings of the 9th Inter. Conf. on SSNTD (Munich, 1976), edited by F. Granzer, E. Schopper and H.G. Paretzche, Pergamon Press (1978)</ref>

From 1977 to 1980, Mubarakmand conducted research on the use of lasers and on isotope [[Isotope separation|separation]] in [[sulfur hexafluoride|sulphur hexafluoride]]. He also studied methods of transmitting signals through [[optical fibers|optical fibres]] to reduce electromagnetic interference. These studies formed part of the broader development of fibre‑optic technology in Pakistan during that period.<ref>11. Citation – “Transmission of Fast Interference Free Signals Through Optical Fibers.” Award of Sitara‑i‑Imtiaz by the Government of Pakistan, 1992, to Dr. Samar Mubarakmand</ref>

===1971 War and Atomic Bomb Project===
In the 1980s, PAEC was busy developing several designs of [[Nuclear weapon|nuclear devices]] and decided that these designs would have to be ratified through [[Nuclear weapons testing#Alternatives to full-scale testing|cold tests]]. Mubarakmand was associated with fast neutron spectrometry.{{Citation needed|date=May 2025}}

Munir Khan, chairman of the PAEC, selected Mubarakmand as the first choice for head of the Diagnostic Group.<ref>12.Pakistan's Pathway to the Bomb - Ambitions, Politics, and Rivalries - Georgetown University Press (2022), Chapter 8, “The Cold Tests: Taking the Gadget for a Ride” Page 194, Mansoor Ahmed</ref>

{{Reduced pull quote|right|"My eyes were set on the mountain in which the test was to be conducted. I experienced a halt in my heartbeat on seeing nothing happening after 32 seconds. But all of a sudden it was a big jolt! We had triumphed....!"|Samar Mubarakmand's describing the [[Nuclear weapon yield|blast yield]] in 1998.|Cited source<ref>{{Cite web |title= Dr. Samar Mubarak Mand |work = Nazari-a-Pakistan |publisher=Nazaria-i-Pakistan |url= http://nazariapak.info/famous-pakistanis/Scientists.html#Mand|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100113154236/http://www.nazariapak.info/famous-pakistanis/Scientists.html#Mand |url-status= dead |archive-date = 13 January 2010|access-date= 26 December 2016}}</ref>}}

Several designs of nuclear devices were developed, and their performance was evaluated with a high degree of confidence through cold testing. Many of the tests involved the detection and measurement of fast neutrons emitted in brief bursts lasting less than a microsecond. All developed device designs were subsequently subjected to cold testing and evaluation. In addition, the Diagnostic Group successfully carried out the important task of designing and manufacturing a neutron trigger source<ref>13.	Pakistan's Pathway to the Bomb - Ambitions, Politics, and Rivalries - Georgetown University Press (2022), Chapter 8, “The Cold Tests: Taking the Gadget for a Ride” Page 190, Mansoor Ahmed</ref> based on fusion reactions. This neutron source would trigger a nuclear device in a hot test.

From 1991 to 1994, Mubarakmand headed the Directorate of Technical Development (DTD). During this period, the directorate developed smaller nuclear devices for use with fighter aircraft and other delivery systems, with designs validated through cold testing.

After three years as Director DTD, Mubarakmand was promoted to Director General DTD in 1994. In 1995, he was given the responsibility of Member Technical [[Pakistan Atomic Energy Commission|PAEC]], which he held until the year 2000. During the five-year tenure, Mubarakmand, apart from looking after the classified side of the Technical Program of PAEC, also became responsible for the optimal functioning of the centres of [[Nuclear medicine|Nuclear Medicine]], Agriculture, [[Pakistan Institute of Nuclear Science & Technology|PINSTECH]], and New Labs. At New Labs, Mubarakmand and a team of PAEC’s Scientists and Engineers were able to establish and commission Pakistan’s first reprocessing plant for burnt reactor fuel. This led to the production of metallic [[plutonium]] at the facility in the year 2000.<ref>14.	Pakistan's Pathway to the Bomb - Ambitions, Politics, and Rivalries - Georgetown University Press (2022) Conclusion, pages 258,260, Mansoor Ahmed</ref>

Several areas were visited and studied with the help of senior [[geologist]]s of the PAEC. Chairman [[Ishfaq Ahmed (politician)|Ishfaq Ahmed]] eventually selected the Chaghai site for conducting Pakistan’s nuclear hot tests. Mubarakmand supervised the installation of diagnostic equipment and other [[Nuclear weapons testing|nuclear testing]] safety infrastructure.

In 2005, Mubarakmand eulogized his memories in an interview with [[Hamid Mir]]'s ''[[Capital Talk]]'' television show and said:

{{blockquote|text="I visited the first [[Ras Koh Hills|weapon-testing laboratories]] (WTL) at ([[Chagai Hills|Chagai District]]) for the first time in 1981.... When the science experiments were to be conducted, our science teams went there on 20th May, and again on 28th May, in the early morning, the WTL iron-steel tunnels were (electronically) plugged in and the preparation for the tests' experiments were complete, and on 28th May, around 15:15hrs, was the time selected for testings. So, at that time, at around 14:45hrs, some of our high profiled guests arrived to witness the (science) experiments that were soon to be tests, and Qadeer Khan was also one of them.... It was the first visit of his life to any of Chagai's Weapon-testing laboratories. (Abdul Qadeer) came at the invitation of the Chairman of the PAEC, [[Ishfaq Ahmad]], and (Abdul Qadeer) arrived 15 minutes prior to the (science) experiments that were to be conducted..."|sign=Samar Mubarakmand, <small>commenting on Abdul Qadeer Khan's role in atomic bomb project</small>|source=<ref name="PakDef, Hamid Mir">{{cite web|author=Hamid Mir|title=Geo News Capital Talk Special: Interview with Dr. Samar Mubarakmand|url=http://pakdef.org/geo-tv-capital-talk-special-interview-with-dr-samar-mubarakmand-n-i-h-i-s-i-chairman-nescom/|publisher=PakDef, Hamid Mir|access-date=3 June 2015|date=3 May 2004|archive-date=19 September 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190919113940/http://pakdef.org/geo-tv-capital-talk-special-interview-with-dr-samar-mubarakmand-n-i-h-i-s-i-chairman-nescom/|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name="[[Geo News]]">{{cite AV media | author =Hamid Mir | title =Capital Talk: Interview with Dr. Samar Mubarakmand | medium =Television production | publisher =[[Geo News]] | location =Islamabad, Pakistan | date =3 May 2005 | url =https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TvAvsNaG7cE | access-date =3 June 2015 | archive-date =10 March 2016 | archive-url =https://web.archive.org/web/20160310131937/https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TvAvsNaG7cE | url-status =live }}</ref>}}

Recalling [[Munir Ahmad Khan]] and the PAEC's role in relation to the atomic bomb project priority dispute, Mubarakmand later said that:

{{blockquote|text="As many as nineteen steps were involved in the making of a nuclear weapon ranging from exploration of uranium to the finished device and its trigger mechanism. The technological and manpower infrastructure for eighteen out of these nineteen steps were provided by PAEC under the leadership of Munir Ahmad Khan who led it for nearly two decades from 1972 to 1991. Today all the major key scientific organizations linked to the country's security like PAEC, the Kahuta Research Labs and the strategic production complex were run and operated by Pakistani professionals produced by the policies of PAEC both under him and Usmani of producing indigenous trained manpower. Pakistan's nuclear capability was confirmed the day in 1983 when PAEC carried out cold nuclear tests under the guidance and stewardship of Munir Ahmad Khan.  The tests however, were not publicly announced because of the international environment of stiff sanctions against countries, which sought to acquire nuclear capability...."|sign=Samar Mubarakmand, <small>Eulogizing Munir Khan's and PAEC's role on the development of the atomic bomb project</small>|source=<ref>{{cite news|last=Mubarakmand|first=Samar|title=Pakistan Became a Nuclear State in 1983|newspaper=The Nation|date=6 August 2009}}</ref>}}

=== Pakistan’s missile program ===

In the 1990s, Mubarakmand worked to advance the [[Pakistan space program|space program]] and led a team of [[engineer]]s that developed the ''[[Shaheen-I]]'' missile.<ref>{{Cite news|work=Nuclear Threat Initiative|title=See: 17 December 2003 (Pakistan to Test Latest Engine for Ghauri IV Missile)|url=http://www.nti.org/e_research/profiles/Pakistan/Missile/3068_4693.html |access-date=26 December 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100411113421/http://www.nti.org/e_research/profiles/Pakistan/Missile/3068_4693.html |archive-date=11 April 2010|url-status=dead}}</ref> He was the founding director of the [[National Defence Complex]] (NDC), which initiated work on the ''Shaheen‑I'' and garnered support for the program.<ref name="Khalid Hanif, special report on Jang, published by FAS">{{cite web|last1=Khalid|first1=Hanif|title=How Shaheen Was Developed|url=http://fas.org/news/pakistan/1999/fbis-nes-1999-0422.htm|publisher=Khalid Hanif, special report on Jang, published by FAS|access-date=4 June 2015|date=19 April 1999}}</ref> Funding for the program was secured by the [[Pakistan Armed Forces|military]], and Mubarakmand oversaw the development of the [[solid-fuel rocket]] booster.<ref name="Khalid Hanif, special report on Jang, published by FAS" />

Initiated in 1987 by the [[Pakistan Ministry of Defence]] in response to India's [[Integrated Guided Missile Development Programme]], Pakistan’s [[Pakistani missile research and development program|spin‑off missile program]] was further pursued in 1993 under Prime Minister [[Benazir Bhutto]]. The ''Shaheen‑I'' missile was test‑fired in 1999 by a team of engineers led by Mubarakmand.<ref name="Khalid Hanif, special report on Jang, published by FAS" /> Subsequently, ''[[Shaheen-II]]'' and ''[[Shaheen-III]]'' were test‑fired, with ranges of 2,000&nbsp;km and 2,750&nbsp;km, respectively.<ref>CSIS: 1616 Rhode Island Avenue NW, Washington, D.C., U.S.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Center_for_Strategic_and_International_Studies {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240604170532/https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Center_for_Strategic_and_International_Studies |date=4 June 2024 }}</ref>

Other strategic systems, including ''[[Babur missile|Babur]]'' and ''[[Ghaznavi (missile)|Ghaznavi]]'', were also developed by teams he led.<ref>{{Cite video| author=Samar Mubarak Mand| title =Samar Mubarakmand- Babur Cruise Missile| url =https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-8OnJLoRhmo| medium =TV-Series| publisher =[[Geo News|Geo TV]]| location =[[Islamabad]] | date = 2006}}</ref> Development of the ''[[Babur (cruise missile)|Babur]]'' cruise missile (range ~700&nbsp;km)<ref>CSIS: 1616 Rhode Island Avenue NW, Washington, D.C., U.S. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Center_for_Strategic_and_International_Studies {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240604170532/https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Center_for_Strategic_and_International_Studies |date=4 June 2024 }}</ref> proceeded in the same period; multiple boost‑phase and flight‑phase tests evaluated performance and potential roles in national defence strategy. Mubarakmand retired from the [[National Engineering & Scientific Commission|NESCOM]] in November 2007.

In 2008, he joined the [[Planning Commission of Pakistan]], where he advocated for peaceful uses of the space program. In 2009, he announced work on [[Paksat-1R]], the country's first [[geostationary satellite]], which was launched in 2011.<ref>{{Cite news | title=Pakistan's first satellite to be launch on April 2011: Dr. Samar | newspaper=[[The News International]] | location=[[Islamabad]]| publisher=The news international| date=18 August 2009| url=http://www.thenews.com.pk/updates.asp?id=85207| access-date=26 December 2016 }}</ref> The satellite was described as supporting monitoring of agriculture, mineral resources, and weather conditions; he also stated that there were sufficient funds for defence, nuclear, and space programs.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.globalsecurity.org/space/world/pakistan/pakistan-shaheen-iii-space-booster.htm|title=Launch Vehicles: Pakistan Shaheen-III Space Booster Development|website=Global Security|access-date=17 June 2019}}</ref> It was launched in 2011 from the [[Xichang Satellite Launch Centre]] in China.<ref name="Dawn, 2011">{{cite news|url=http://www.dawn.com/2011/08/11/pakistans-first-communications-satellite-paksat-1r-launched.html|title=Pakistan's First Communications Satellite PakSat-1R Launched.|date=11 August 2011|access-date=4 June 2015|publisher=Dawn, 2011|agency=Dawn|archive-date=24 February 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120224101933/http://www.dawn.com/2011/08/11/pakistans-first-communications-satellite-paksat-1r-launched.html|url-status=dead}}</ref> His relations with [[Dr. Abdul Qadeer Khan|Dr Abdul Qadeer Khan]] were often tense over scientific issues.

===Thar Coal Project===
{{Main|Thar coalfield|Reko Diq}}

In 2013, Mubarakmand assisted the [[Government of Balochistan, Pakistan|Provincial Government of Balochistan]] in [[mineral extraction]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://nation.com.pk/31-Jan-2013/balochistan-set-to-undertake-reko-diq-project|title=Balochistan set to undertake Reko Diq project|date=31 January 2013|website=The Nation|language=en|access-date=17 June 2019|archive-date=17 June 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190617064428/https://nation.com.pk/31-Jan-2013/balochistan-set-to-undertake-reko-diq-project|url-status=live}}</ref> He lobbied heavily for the implementation of the [[Thar coalfield|Thar coal project]] initiated by the [[Government of Sindh|Provincial Government of Sindh]] despite strong public criticism by [[Abdul Qadeer Khan]]. In 2015, a breakthrough in the Thar coal project was reported by the media.<ref name="Dawn News, Kiani"/> According to Mubarakmand, the Thar coal reserves have been projected to supply power for several decades, subject to development and policy implementation. When speaking to a large crowd at [[Cadet College Fateh Jang]], he said that he had developed a solution to the growing power outage and was now waiting for the government to put it into action.<ref>{{cite web |last= |first= |date= |title=No more load shedding if power generated from coal in Thar: Dr. Mubarak |url=https://www.samaaenglish.tv/news/354831 |website=Samaa Tv |location=Lahore, Pakistan |publisher=[[Samaa TV]] |url-status= |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230406011132/https://www.samaaenglish.tv/news/354831 |archive-date=6 April 2023 |access-date=2 January 2026}}</ref>

===Reko Diq Copper Gold Project===
{{Main|Reko Diq case}}

In December 2020, the Tethyan Cooper Company (TCC) approached the [[High Court of Justice]] in the British Virgin Islands for the enforcement of the $5.97 billion award against [[Pakistan]] by the [[International Centre for Settlement of Investment Disputes]] (ICSID) in the [[Reko Diq case]].<ref name="Dawn News">{{cite news|title=Mining firm moves Virgin Islands court for enforcement of Reko Diq award against Pakistan|url=https://www.dawn.com/news/1597596/mining-firm-moves-virgin-islands-court-for-enforcement-of-reko-diq-award-against-pakistan|access-date=24 December 2020|agency=Dawn News|publisher=Dawn News|date=24 December 2020}}</ref>

A senior official revealed that the "misstatement" of Mubarakmand before the Supreme Court tribunal, in which he in 2011 had claimed that the [[Reko Diq Mine|Reko Diq]] gold mines would fetch Pakistan around $2.5 billion annually, was one of the main reasons behind the Supreme Court's decision on 7 January 2013. On that date, a three-member bench of the apex court, headed by then Chief Justice [[Iftikhar Chaudhry|Iftikhar Muhammad Chaudhry]], declared the Chagai Hills Exploration Joint Venture Agreement (Chejva) "illegal, void" and non-binding, causing the ICSID to penalize Pakistan. Mubarakmand projected that Reko Diq and other reserves could generate up to $131 billion over the mine’s lifetime.<ref>Submission by Dr. Samar Mubarakmand in the Supreme Court of Pakistan Constitution Petition No. 68 of 2010</ref> The tribunal relied on his statement.<ref>{{cite news|title=Reko Diq case:Ex-CJP's verdict costs Pakistan $6b|url=https://tribune.com.pk/story/2013028/1-reko-diq-case-ex-cjps-verdict-costs-pakistan-6b|access-date=24 December 2020|agency=The Express Tribune|publisher=The Express Tribune|date=14 July 2019}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Reko Diq mines: Pakistan can earn $2b a year, scientist tells court|url=https://tribune.com.pk/story/103120/reko-diq-mines-pakistan-can-earn-2b-a-year-scientist-tells-court|access-date=25 December 2020|agency=The Express Tribune|publisher=The Express Tribune|date=13 January 2011}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Magic mountains: The Reko Diq gold and copper mining project|url=https://herald.dawn.com/news/1153283|access-date=25 December 2020|agency=The Express Herald|publisher=Herald|date=29 September 2017}}</ref><ref name="Dawn News" />

==State honors==
{{BLP sources section|date=May 2024}}
Mubarakmand has been conferred with [[Civil decorations of Pakistan|state honors]] for his services to the country by the [[Government of Pakistan]]. He is the recipient of the [[Sitara-e-Imtiaz]] (1992); [[Hilal-e-Imtiaz]] (1998); and the [[Nishan-e-Imtiaz]] (2003), which is the highest civil honor of Pakistan.<ref name="Pakistan Academy of Sciences" /><ref>{{Cite web|last= Asim|first= Khalid Mahmood|title = Dr. Samar Mubarak Mand|website= Nazari-a-Pak |url= http://nazariapak.info/famous-pakistanis/Scientists.html#Mand|archive-url  = https://web.archive.org/web/20100113154236/http://www.nazariapak.info/famous-pakistanis/Scientists.html#Mand|url-status = dead|archive-date = 13 January 2010|access-date   = 26 December 2016}}</ref> Additionally, he is a [[Fellow of the Pakistan Academy of Sciences]] (PAS), inducted by [[Ishfaq Ahmad]] in 2000.<ref name="Pakistan Academy of Sciences" /><ref>{{cite web | title=Dr. Samar Mubarakmand (NI, HI, SI) &#124; Punjab Mineral Company | url=https://pmc.punjab.gov.pk/dr_samar_mubarakmand | access-date=4 September 2025 | archive-date=7 August 2024 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240807080845/https://pmc.punjab.gov.pk/dr_samar_mubarakmand | url-status=live }}</ref>
